SALT DEDUCTION CAP CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's your SALT deduction actually capped at?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act raised the SALT (state and local tax) itemized deduction cap to $40,000 for 2025 — but above $500,000 of MAGI, that increase phases back down at 30 cents per dollar, never below a $10,000 floor. This tool applies the exact 2025 or 2026 cap, threshold, and phase-out for your filing status to your own numbers.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status and tax year

Married filing separately gets a halved cap and threshold, not a per-person share of the joint figures. Single, head of household, and married filing jointly all share the same cap and threshold.

2. Your numbers

MAGI is close to AGI for most filers — this tool does not compute it for you. State and local taxes paid means property tax plus state income tax (or sales tax, if you elect that instead), the total before any cap is applied.

Fill in your filing status, MAGI, and taxes paid, then click Calculate.

Your SALT cap

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This computes one cap on one deduction — not total itemized deductions, whether itemizing beats the standard deduction, other credits, AMT, or state tax.
  • Does not compute MAGI. You supply MAGI directly; this tool does not derive it from wages, business income, or other add-backs.
  • No pass-through entity tax (PTET) modeling. A PTET election can let a pass-through business owner deduct state tax above this individual cap entirely — flagged, not computed.
  • 2025 and 2026 only. The cap is scheduled to increase 1% per year through 2029, then revert to $10,000 in 2030 — those years are out of scope here.

Common questions

What is the SALT deduction cap, and did it really go up?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, temporarily raised the SALT (state and local tax) itemized deduction cap from $10,000 ($5,000 married filing separately) to $40,000 ($20,000 MFS) for 2025, increasing 1% per year through 2029 — $40,400 ($20,200 MFS) for 2026. In 2030 the cap is scheduled to revert to $10,000 ($5,000 MFS) unless Congress acts again.

Is the $40,000 cap the same for single, head of household, and married filing jointly?

Yes. Single, head-of-household, and married-filing-jointly filers all get the same $40,000 (2025) / $40,400 (2026) cap and the same $500,000 (2025) / $505,000 (2026) phase-out threshold — a joint return does not get double the single amount. Only married filing separately gets a different, exactly-halved figure: a $20,000/$20,200 cap phasing out above $250,000/$252,500 MAGI.

How does the phase-out work?

Once modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds the threshold, the increased cap is reduced by 30 cents for every dollar of MAGI above it — not a cliff, and not a percentage of the cap itself. The reduction stops once the cap reaches its floor: $10,000 for most filers, $5,000 for married filing separately. That floor point is $600,000 MAGI in 2025 for single/HOH/MFJ ($300,000 MFS), and roughly $606,333/$303,167 in 2026.

Can my SALT deduction ever drop below $10,000?

No. The phase-out only removes the OBBBA increase above the permanent-law floor — $10,000 for most filers ($5,000 married filing separately) — which every itemizing filer keeps regardless of income. This is the same amount the cap has been since the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act; OBBBA's phase-out cannot push it any lower.

Does this account for a pass-through entity tax (PTET) election?

No. Several states let a partnership or S corporation elect to pay state tax at the entity level, which the owner's share can then deduct above this individual cap entirely. This calculator estimates the cap on state and local tax paid directly by an individual filer — it does not model a PTET election's effect, which can materially change the picture for a pass-through business owner.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal SALT cap and phase-out rules to the numbers you enter. It does not compute your MAGI, verify your filing status, or model state-specific PTET elections, and it is not a substitute for reviewing IRS guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers and elections before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Own part of an S corporation or partnership? See the PTE tax election calculator — whether a state pass-through entity tax election gets around this cap, or costs you money.

Turning 65 (or married to someone who is) instead? See the senior deduction calculator — a different new OBBBA deduction, phased fully to zero rather than floored like this one. Also giving to charity in 2026? See the charitable deduction calculator — another new itemized-deduction floor, this one on charitable giving rather than state and local tax.

Working this out by hand instead? See where a hand estimate of the SALT cap phase-out usually goes wrong. Wondering whether a bigger cap actually helps your refund? See is the SALT deduction worth itemizing for? — sometimes none of it is.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Is the SALT deduction worth itemizing for?

Sometimes none of it -- even after OBBBA raised the cap to $40,000.

The calculator on this page's own index tells you your SALT deduction after the cap and phase-out. That figure is real, but it answers a narrower question than "does this help my refund." It only helps once your total itemized deductions -- SALT plus mortgage interest, charitable gifts, and anything else you itemize -- clear your standard deduction. And even then, only the slice that pushes you past the standard deduction is SALT's own contribution; the rest just matches ground the standard deduction covers for free.

The arithmetic in one line

Compare two totals: what you'd claim with SALT in the mix, and what you'd claim without it -- each the larger of itemizing or the standard deduction:

FigureFormula
Best claim with SALTmax(other itemized + SALT deduction, standard deduction)
Best claim without SALTmax(other itemized alone, standard deduction)
SALT's marginal benefitthe difference between the two

That difference can land anywhere from $0 (SALT changes nothing) up to the full capped SALT deduction (SALT is entirely extra savings) -- which of those you get depends entirely on your other itemized deductions, not on the SALT figure alone.

Three filers, three outcomes -- all pinned against the calculator's own arithmetic

All three use the 2025 rules. Filing status and MAGI only decide the SALT cap and phase-out (via the same saltCapOutcome() the calculator uses); the standard deduction depends only on filing status and tax year.

Fully additive Married filing jointly, $35,000 of other itemized deductions

MAGI $200,000 (below the $500,000 phase-out threshold, so the cap is unreduced), $12,000 of state and local tax paid -- fully deductible, since it's under the $40,000 cap. $35,000 of mortgage interest and charitable gifts already clears the $31,500 married-filing-jointly standard deduction on its own.

ItemAmount
SALT deduction (capped)$12,000
Other itemized deductions$35,000
Total itemized$47,000
Standard deduction (MFJ, 2025)$31,500
Best claim without SALTmax($35,000, $31,500) = $35,000
Best claim with SALTmax($47,000, $31,500) = $47,000
SALT's marginal benefit$12,000 -- every dollar

Partly additive Same couple, only $20,000 of other itemized deductions

Identical SALT deduction, same $200,000 MAGI -- only the mortgage interest and charitable total changes, to $20,000, which alone falls short of the $31,500 standard deduction.

ItemAmount
SALT deduction (capped)$12,000
Other itemized deductions$20,000
Total itemized$32,000
Standard deduction (MFJ, 2025)$31,500
Best claim without SALTmax($20,000, $31,500) = $31,500 (the standard deduction)
Best claim with SALTmax($32,000, $31,500) = $32,000
SALT's marginal benefit$500 -- not $12,000

$11,500 of this filer's $12,000 SALT deduction just closes the gap between their $20,000 of other itemized deductions and the $31,500 standard deduction they would have taken anyway. Only the last $500 is money the SALT deduction actually saved them.

Wholly absorbed Single filer, $3,000 of other itemized deductions

MAGI $100,000, $8,000 of state and local tax paid (all deductible -- nowhere near the $40,000 cap). Only $3,000 of other itemized deductions.

ItemAmount
SALT deduction (capped)$8,000
Other itemized deductions$3,000
Total itemized$11,000
Standard deduction (single, 2025)$15,750
Best claim without SALTmax($3,000, $15,750) = $15,750
Best claim with SALTmax($11,000, $15,750) = $15,750
SALT's marginal benefit$0

This filer takes the standard deduction either way. Their $8,000 SALT deduction is real, correctly computed, and nowhere near the OBBBA cap -- and it adds exactly nothing to their refund, because their total itemized deductions never clear the $15,750 standard deduction.

Run your own numbers

The SALT deduction cap calculator computes the capped SALT figure this page uses as an input. It does not ask for your other itemized deductions or compare against the standard deduction -- that comparison is what this page walks through by hand. Nothing you enter anywhere on this site is uploaded.

Common questions

Does a bigger SALT cap always mean a bigger tax benefit?

No. The SALT deduction only helps at all if your total itemized deductions -- SALT plus mortgage interest, charitable gifts, and anything else you itemize -- exceed your standard deduction. If they don't, you take the standard deduction instead and the SALT cap, however generous, contributes nothing to your refund.

What does "partly additive" mean?

It means only part of your SALT deduction is genuine extra savings. If your other itemized deductions alone fall short of the standard deduction, the first slice of your SALT deduction just closes that gap -- matching ground the standard deduction already covered for free. Only the remainder, the part that pushes your total itemized deductions past the standard deduction, is SALT's own contribution.

What does "wholly absorbed" mean?

It means your SALT deduction, even after the OBBBA cap and phase-out are applied, adds nothing: your other itemized deductions plus SALT still don't exceed the standard deduction, so you take the standard deduction either way and the marginal benefit of the SALT deduction is zero.

Why doesn't the calculator's own "deduction" figure answer this?

The calculator's deductible amount is the SALT-specific figure after the cap and phase-out -- a real number, but only half the picture. It says nothing about your other itemized deductions or the standard deduction, so a large capped SALT deduction can still add zero to your actual refund once the standard-deduction comparison is applied, exactly as the wholly-absorbed example on this page shows.

Is this tax advice?

No. This page applies the published 2025/2026 standard deduction figures and ordinary itemize-vs-standard arithmetic to numbers you supply. It does not know your other itemized deductions, verify your filing status, or replace a qualified tax professional -- confirm your own numbers before filing.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal statutory figures and ordinary itemize-vs-standard-deduction arithmetic to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own filing status, MAGI, and other itemized deductions before filing. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. working out the SALT cap phase-out by hand

The arithmetic looks simple — 30 cents per dollar over a threshold. The part that goes wrong by hand is the shape of the rule: which filing statuses share a cap, where the reduction stops, and what it is a percentage of.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Filing-status capAssumes a joint return gets double the single cap.Uses the correct shared $40,000/$40,400 figure for single, HOH, and MFJ alike, and the separately-halved MFS figure.
Where the phase-out stopsKeeps subtracting 30% of excess MAGI past the point where the cap would go negative.Floors the effective cap at $10,000 ($5,000 MFS) and shows the exact MAGI where that floor is reached.
What the 30% applies toApplies the reduction to income or to taxes paid, rather than to the cap.Reduces the CAP by 30 cents per dollar of MAGI above the threshold, then applies that cap to taxes paid.
Pass-through entity taxOnly checks the personal SALT cap, missing a state PTET election that could deduct more through a business.Flags the PTET caveat explicitly as out of scope, so it is not silently assumed away.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Assuming a married-filing-jointly return gets double the single cap — it does not. Single, head-of-household, and married-filing-jointly filers all share the exact same $40,000 (2025) / $40,400 (2026) cap and $500,000/$505,000 threshold. Only married filing separately gets a different, halved figure.

What's the second most common mistake?

Assuming the phase-out eventually takes the deduction to zero. It does not — the cap can never drop below its permanent-law floor of $10,000 ($5,000 married filing separately), no matter how high MAGI goes. A hand estimate that keeps subtracting 30% of excess MAGI past that point understates the deduction.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Applying the 30% reduction to the WRONG base — to total income rather than to the excess above the threshold, or to the taxes-paid figure rather than to the cap itself. The reduction is 30 cents per dollar of MAGI above the threshold, subtracted from the CAP, not from the amount of tax paid.

What planning mistake gets made most often?

Not checking whether a pass-through entity tax (PTET) election is available. Several states let a partnership or S corporation pay state tax at the entity level, letting the owner deduct that share above this individual cap entirely — a hand estimate that only looks at the personal SALT cap can miss a substantially larger deduction already available through the business.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page computes your MAGI, knows whether itemizing beats your standard deduction, or models a state's PTET election. Both apply the same published federal cap and phase-out rules to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.
